title: Electrochemistry
summary: Learn about cells, electrode potentials, the Nernst equation, electrolysis, Faraday's law and corrosion.
cards.0.p: If you connect two half-cells with a wire and a salt bridge, electrons flow through the wire. This setup is called a galvanic cell. The Zn electrode, which is oxidized, is the anode and the − terminal. The electrode where Cu2+ is reduced is the cathode and the + terminal.
cards.0.etk.soru: Tap the parts of the Daniell cell.
cards.0.etk.noktalar.0.acik: Zn atoms give electrons and go into solution as Zn²⁺. This is oxidation.
cards.0.etk.noktalar.1.acik: Cu²⁺ ions take the electrons from the wire and build up as copper. This is reduction.
cards.0.etk.noktalar.2.acik: Electrons flow only through the wire. The voltmeter reads 1.10 V.
cards.0.etk.noktalar.3.acik: The salt bridge balances the charges by carrying ions. Anions go to the anode and cations to the cathode.
cards.0.etk.noktalar.4.acik: As the cell runs, the Zn²⁺ concentration rises.
cards.0.etk.noktalar.5.acik: As Cu²⁺ decreases, the blue color of the solution fades.
cards.0.key: If you drop Zn straight into CuSO₄, the energy comes out only as heat. As the cell runs, the Zn gets thinner and the Cu gets thicker.
cards.1.p: The salt bridge balances the charges. Anions go to the anode and cations to the cathode. Without the bridge the current stops. This cell is written as Zn | Zn2+ || Cu2+ | Cu.
cards.1.svg#19: single line (|): boundary between solid and solution
cards.1.key: The anode is written on the left, and the double line is the salt bridge. Electrons travel only through the wire, and ions through the solution and the bridge.
cards.2.p: The voltage of a single half-cell can't be measured. So the voltage of the standard hydrogen electrode is taken as 0.00 V. The reduction potential measured against it is called E°. If E° is large, the ion is easily reduced.
cards.2.svg#21: Strong oxidizing agents on top, active metals at the bottom
cards.2.key: Measurements are made at 25 °C, 1 M and 1 atm. Active metals have negative E° values.
cards.2.once.soru: E° = −0.76 V for Zn²⁺/Zn and +0.34 V for Cu²⁺/Cu. Which ion is reduced more easily?
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: The ion with the larger E° takes electrons more easily.
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: A negative E° shows that the ion is hard to reduce.
cards.3.p: The standard cell voltage is E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. For the Daniell cell it is 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V. If E°cell is positive, the reaction is spontaneous, meaning it runs on its own.
cards.3.svg#8: If an oxidation potential is given
cards.3.svg#11: If E° < 0, the reverse reaction is spontaneous
cards.3.key: Even if you multiply a half-reaction by a number, E° stays the same. If a question gives an oxidation potential, flip its sign.
cards.4.p: At 25 °C, E = E° − (0.0592/n)·log Q. For the Daniell cell, Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]. E is changed by concentration and temperature. The mass of the electrodes and the volume of solution don't change E.
cards.4.key: Raising the concentration of the ion at the cathode or lowering that of the ion at the anode raises the voltage. If [Zn²⁺] is 0.01 M and [Cu²⁺] is 1 M, E is about 1.16 V.
cards.4.once.soru: You add more Cu²⁺ to the cathode beaker of a Daniell cell. What happens to the cell voltage?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: When the reactant ion increases, Q gets smaller and E gets larger.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: The voltage falls when the product ion, Zn²⁺, increases.
cards.5.p: Current flows even when the two half-cells are the same but the concentrations differ. This is called a concentration cell. The dilute side is the anode, where Cu dissolves. The concentrated side is the cathode, where Cu2+ is reduced.
cards.5.key: For 0.01 M and 1 M solutions at 25 °C, E is about 0.059 V. When the concentrations become equal, the voltage drops to zero.
cards.5.once.soru: One beaker holds 0.01 M Cu²⁺ and the other 1 M, each with a Cu rod. Does current flow?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: The concentrations differ, so Q ≠ 1 and E is not zero. Current flows until the concentrations become equal.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: E° is zero, but E depends on concentration.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: Current flows at room temperature too.
cards.6.h: Why does a battery go dead?
cards.6.p: As the cell runs, Zn2+ builds up and Cu2+ decreases. So Q rises and E falls. In the end equilibrium is reached, with Q = K and E = 0. The cell is dead, but E° doesn't change.
cards.6.svg#6: Zn²⁺ builds up, Cu²⁺ falls → Q grows
cards.6.key: E° is a fixed value for standard conditions, and it doesn't change as the cell runs down.
cards.6.once.soru: Are the electrodes of a dead battery used up?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: A cell goes dead when the reaction reaches equilibrium. The electrodes may still be there.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: What makes a cell dead is the voltage dropping to zero.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: While the cell runs, the anode gets thinner and the cathode thicker.
cards.7.p: Driving a nonspontaneous redox reaction with an external source is called electrolysis. In an electrolytic cell the anode is the + terminal and the cathode is −. But oxidation still happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode.
cards.7.svg#14: Oxidation always happens at the anode; only the sign changes.
cards.7.key: Electrical energy turns into chemical energy. In a galvanic cell the anode is −, and in electrolysis the anode is +.
cards.7.once.soru: What happens to the reaction in the battery while you charge your phone?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: The charger supplies energy from outside and drives the nonspontaneous direction. This is electrolysis.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: The direction that runs on its own is the battery discharging.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: During charging, the reaction runs in reverse.
cards.8.h: Electrolysis of molten NaCl and water
cards.8.p: When molten NaCl is electrolyzed, Na metal forms at the cathode and Cl₂ gas at the anode. Pure water conducts current poorly. Adding a little H₂SO₄ to water makes it conduct, and the water splits into H₂ and O₂.
cards.8.key: In aqueous NaCl solution, H₂ comes out at the cathode instead of Na, because water is reduced much more easily than Na⁺.
cards.9.p: In aqueous solution, water also competes. At the cathode, Cu²⁺ and Ag⁺ build up as metal. Instead of 1A, 2A and Al³⁺ ions, water is reduced. At the anode, Cl⁻ is oxidized, but instead of SO₄²⁻, water is oxidized.
cards.9.key: Br⁻ and I⁻ are also oxidized at the anode. Instead of NO₃⁻, water is oxidized and O₂ comes out. When concentrated NaCl is electrolyzed, NaOH is left in the solution.
cards.9.once.soru: Aqueous NaCl solution is electrolyzed. What comes out at the cathode?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: Water is reduced instead of Na⁺, and H₂ comes out at the cathode.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: Na metal is obtained only from molten NaCl.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: Cl₂ comes out at the anode.
cards.10.p: In plating, the object to be plated is the cathode and the plating metal is the anode. In refining, impure copper is the anode and pure copper the cathode. Ag and Au don't dissolve and settle as anode mud.
cards.10.key: The object to be plated is always connected to the − end of the source. The solution contains ions of the plating metal.
cards.10.once.soru: You want to plate a spoon with silver. Which electrode do you make the spoon?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: Ag⁺ is reduced at the cathode and builds up as metal. So the spoon must be the cathode.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: Metal dissolves at the anode. If the spoon were the anode, it would get thinner.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: Plating builds up only at the cathode.
cards.11.p: The charge passing through the circuit is Q = I·t. The charge of 1 mol of electrons is called 1 faraday, about 96 500 C. Cu2+ takes 2e−, so 0.1 mol of e− deposits 0.05 mol of Cu.
cards.11.svg#9: Same charge: 0.1 mol metal from Ag⁺, 0.05 mol from Cu²⁺
cards.11.etk.soru: Current passes through CuSO₄ solution: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Change the current and the time. (1 F ≈ 96 500 C, Cu = 63.5 g/mol)
cards.11.key: If a 9.65 A current flows for 1000 s, it carries 9650 C, or 0.1 mol of e⁻. This charge deposits about 3.2 g of Cu. The same charge passes through cells connected in series.
cards.12.p: Rusting is a cell that runs on its own. Fe is oxidized, and O₂ is reduced together with water. Paint and galvanizing (zinc coating) protect iron. Mg connected to iron acts as a sacrificial anode.
cards.12.svg#1: center: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ (a pit forms here)
cards.12.key: Rusting needs water and oxygen. Salt raises conductivity and speeds up rusting. The formula of rust is Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.
cards.13.p: In a dry cell, Zn is the anode and MnO₂ the cathode, giving ≈1.5 V. A lead-acid battery cell gives ≈2 V, and six cells give 12 V. In a lithium-ion battery, Li+ moves back and forth.
cards.13.svg#21: While charging, the battery is an electrolytic cell.
cards.13.key: A dry cell can't be recharged. A lead-acid battery works with Pb and PbO₂ electrodes in H₂SO₄. While charging, it acts as an electrolytic cell.
cards.13.once.soru: How many cells are in a car's 12 V battery?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: Each lead-acid cell gives about 2 V. So 6 · 2 = 12 V.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: One cell gives ≈2 V, not 1 V.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: A single cell gives only ≈2 V.
cards.14.p:
• In a galvanic cell, a spontaneous redox reaction produces electricity, and the anode is −.
• E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, and coefficients don't change E°.
• As Q rises, E falls, reaching zero at equilibrium.
• Electrolysis drives a nonspontaneous reaction, and the anode is +.
• Charge is Q = I·t. 1 F ≈ 96 500 C.
quiz.0.q: Two cells are connected in series, one with AgNO₃ solution and the other with CuSO₄. When 5.4 g of Ag deposits at the cathode of the first cell, how many grams of Cu deposit at the cathode of the second? (Ag = 108, Cu = 63.5 g/mol)
quiz.0.e: 5.4 / 108 = 0.05 mol of Ag deposited, so 0.05 mol of e<sup>−</sup> passed. The same charge passes through cells in series. Since Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup> → Cu, 0.025 mol, or 0.025 × 63.5 ≈ 1.59 g of Cu deposits.
quiz.1.q: Sort each property under galvanic cell or electrolytic cell.
quiz.1.e: In a galvanic cell, a spontaneous redox reaction produces electricity and the anode is −. In electrolysis, an external source drives a nonspontaneous reaction, electrical energy turns into chemical energy and the anode is +.
quiz.2.q: For each electrolysis, match the product formed at that electrode.
quiz.2.e: In molten NaCl, Na<sup>+</sup> is reduced and Cl<sup>−</sup> is oxidized. In aqueous solution, Cu<sup>2+</sup> builds up as metal. Instead of Na<sup>+</sup>, water is reduced and gives H₂. Instead of SO₄<sup>2−</sup>, water is oxidized and gives O₂.
quiz.3.q: E° = −0.25 V for Ni<sup>2+</sup>/Ni and +0.80 V for Ag<sup>+</sup>/Ag. What is E° for a cell based on Ni + 2Ag<sup>+</sup> → Ni<sup>2+</sup> + 2Ag?
quiz.3.e: E° = 0.80 − (−0.25) = 1.05 V. Even though the Ag half-reaction is multiplied by 2, E° doesn't change. Using 2·0.80 is a common mistake.
quiz.3.y.0: E° is not multiplied by the coefficient. For Ag<sup>+</sup>, 0.80 V stays as it is, and the result is 0.80 − (−0.25).
quiz.3.y.1: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. Instead of adding −0.25, you must subtract it. The right answer is 0.80 − (−0.25) = 1.05 V.
quiz.3.y.3: You swapped the cathode and the anode. Ag<sup>+</sup> is reduced, Ni is oxidized, and E° = +1.05 V.
A:ozet: Follow the electrons in a Daniell cell and remove the salt bridge. Build cells from standard potentials, electrolyze water and do a Faraday calculation.
A:adimlar.0.metin: A Zn strip stands in ZnSO₄ solution and a Cu strip in CuSO₄ solution. We connected them with a wire and a salt bridge. The cell will run for a while.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: What happens to the strips as the cell runs?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Zn atoms give electrons and go into solution as Zn²⁺. So the strip gets thinner. The electrons travel through the wire to Cu, where Cu²⁺ ions build up as Cu. As Cu²⁺ decreases, the blue color fades too.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Zn is the one that gives electrons. Does an atom that gives away its electrons stay on the strip, or become an ion and go into solution?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The current comes from atoms giving and taking electrons. A Zn atom that has given away its electrons is now an ion and goes into solution.
A:adimlar.1.metin: The cell is running. Remove the salt bridge and look at the voltmeter.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: Without the bridge, the circuit isn't complete. + charge builds up in the anode beaker and − charge in the cathode beaker, and the current stops.
A:adimlar.2.metin: The cell voltage is E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. The half-cell with the larger E° is the cathode. Choose the anode and cathode to build a cell that gives 1.56 V.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.ipucu: Calculate with E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. The current Zn–Cu cell gives 1.10 V.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: With Zn as the anode and Ag as the cathode, you get 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V. The values in the table are measured against the standard hydrogen electrode (0 V). If E° came out negative, the cell wouldn't run on its own.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Ag⁺ takes one electron. To make the electrons equal, we multiplied the Ag half-reaction by 2.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: What is E° for this cell?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: 0.80 − 0.34 = 0.46 V. E° doesn't depend on the amount of substance and isn't multiplied by the coefficient.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: You used 2 · 0.80 − 0.34. E° doesn't depend on amount. Multiplying a half-reaction by 2 doesn't change E°.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: You used 0.80 + 0.34. But you take the difference: E°cathode − E°anode.
A:adimlar.4.metin: We pass current through water with a little electrolyte added.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: H₂ at anode, O₂ at cathode
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The places are swapped. H₂ comes out at the cathode, where electrons are taken. The volumes aren't equal either.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Reduction happens at the cathode and gives H₂. Oxidation happens at the anode and gives O₂. So the gases are different.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: H₂ at cathode, O₂ at anode, twice as much H₂
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: At the cathode water is reduced and H₂ comes out. At the anode water is oxidized and O₂ comes out. Since 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂, the volume of H₂ is twice that of O₂.
A:adimlar.5.metin: A 4 A current passes through CuSO₄ solution. Set the time needed to deposit 0.1 mol of copper at the cathode. (1 F ≈ 96 500 C, Cu = 63.5 g/mol)
A:adimlar.5.gorev.ipucu: 0.1 mol of Cu needs 0.2 mol of electrons. So Q = 0.2 · 96 500 C.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: Q = 0.2 · 96 500 = 19 300 C. t = Q / I = 19 300 / 4 = 4825 s. 6.35 g of copper deposits at the cathode. In plating, the object to be plated is made the cathode.
A:adimlar.6.metin: Of two iron nails, one is coated with tin and the other with zinc. The coating on both nails got scratched, and the scratches are wet with salt water.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Zn is more active than iron. It is oxidized itself and protects the iron. Sn is less active than iron. When the coating is scratched, the iron becomes the anode and rusts faster.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: A coating is a barrier only while it is intact. At a scratch, what matters is which metal becomes the anode.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The opposite happens. Zinc is more active than iron, so it is oxidized first. That is why Mg or Zn blocks are used on ships as sacrificial anodes.
A:kapanis.0: In a galvanic cell, the anode (−) is oxidized and the cathode (+) is reduced. In the external circuit, electrons flow from the anode to the cathode.
A:kapanis.1: The salt bridge keeps the solutions neutral. Without it the current stops.
A:kapanis.2: The cell voltage is E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, and coefficients don't change E°. The Zn–Cu cell gives 1.10 V, and the Cu–Ag cell 0.46 V.
A:kapanis.3: In electrolysis the anode is + and the cathode is −. In the electrolysis of water, H₂ collects at the cathode and half that volume of O₂ at the anode.
A:kapanis.4: The amount deposited is calculated with Q = I·t and 1 F ≈ 96 500 C. Coating with an active metal and sacrificial anodes protect iron from corrosion.
